knownFor: Founded, by tradition, by Birger Jarl in the 1250s
Tre Kronor castle and Storkyrkan, its only medieval parish church
Export of Bergslagen iron and copper through its German merchants
The town every ruler of the Kalmar Union had to hold
Sten Sture's victory over Christian I of Denmark at Brunkeberg in 1471
The Saint George and the Dragon monument of 1489
overview: Stockholm grew up on Stadsholmen, the island where Lake Mälaren drains into the Baltic, around a castle traditionally credited to Birger Jarl. Its German and Swedish merchants shipped the iron and copper of Bergslagen to Lübeck and Danzig, and because the castle and town commanded the whole Mälaren basin, kings, regents and rebels of the Kalmar Union era fought over it again and again.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Stockholm stands on a cluster of islands in the narrow channel through which Lake Mälaren empties into Saltsjön, the arm of the Baltic reaching in from the archipelago. Whoever held the channel controlled shipping to and from the Mälaren towns of Västerås, Arboga and Köping, the outlets of the Bergslagen mines, and the route to Uppsala, seat of Sweden's archbishop. The town first appears in two Latin letters issued by Birger Jarl in 1252, and by 1300 it was the largest town in Sweden.

Its medieval history is the history of that position. German merchants, many from Lübeck, dominated its trade and for long held half the seats on its council, and every king and regent of the Kalmar Union period, from Albert of Mecklenburg to Christian II of Denmark, had to take or keep Stockholm castle to rule the kingdom.

contentSections.title: A lock on Lake Mälaren
paragraphs: The name means something like 'log islet' and has no agreed explanation; the most favoured one points to wooden piles driven into the strait north of the island, which tree-ring dating in the late 1970s placed around the year 1000. The older centres of the Mälaren region, Birka and then Sigtuna, had faded, and a note in the Visby chronicle ties Stockholm's founding to the sack of Sigtuna by eastern raiders in 1187, but that note was written down only around 1410 and is doubted.

The first secure record is a pair of letters issued by Birger Jarl in 1252, one in July protecting the convent at Fogdö and one dated 19 August ordering the people of Attundaland to pay tithe to Uppsala Cathedral. Neither describes the place. The rhymed Erikskrönikan, written in the 1320s, says Birger built Stockholm as a lock to shut the rich Mälaren country against pirates and enemy fleets from the Baltic. Historians still disagree whether the island was mostly farmland in 1250 and grew fast around the new castle or was already a trading place, but commercial treaties with Lübeck in the 1250s and Hamburg in 1261 show that German merchants were wanted there from the start.

contentSections.title: The Folkung town, 1252–1389
paragraphs: The castle began as a tower on the northern high point of the island inside a simple wall and grew over two centuries into the royal castle later called Tre Kronor, after the three crowns on its keep; when the crowns were first put there is not known. Birger's son Magnus III of Sweden, Magnus Ladulås, patronised the Franciscans on the islet west of the town, long called Gråmunkeholmen, Greyfriars Islet, and in 1288 gave them another island from which they cut timber for their church. He was buried in that church in 1290, and parts of it, now Riddarholmen Church, are among the oldest standing buildings in Stockholm.

The town church, dedicated to Saint Nicholas, patron of Baltic seafarers, is first recorded in 1279 and was consecrated in 1306; as Storkyrkan it remained Stockholm's only parish church until the 1590s. Magnus Eriksson and his queen Blanche of Namur made a gift to it in 1346 that probably paid for its first side chapel, and in 1336 he gave the Dominicans the old tower at the island's southern tip, where their Blackfriars convent was consecrated in 1343. In the early fourteenth century the town also won a staple right: goods from Roslagen and the whole Gulf of Bothnia, the furs, hides and fish of Norrland and Finland, could be sold only in Stockholm.

When Swedish nobles turned against Magnus Eriksson and brought in his nephew Albert of Mecklenburg in 1364, Stockholm, with its large German population, welcomed the new king, and in 1371 it held out when Haakon VI of Norway besieged it. Albert later lost the Swedish nobility, and in February 1389 the army of Margaret I of Denmark defeated and captured him at Åsle, but Stockholm stayed in the hands of his German partisans.

contentSections.title: German and Swedish burghers
paragraphs: The town's law gave its German community an extraordinary place. The council was by statute half German and half Swedish, merchants filled nearly every seat, craftsmen were occasionally given minor duties and the rest of the townspeople had no voice. The German merchants lived above all around the grain harbour and the iron market at the island's southern end, where boats from Mälaren unloaded and seagoing cogs loaded for Lübeck and Danzig.

After Åsle that balance broke. In June 1389 members of the German faction called the Hättebröder, the hooded brothers, shut about seventy men of the Swedish party in a barn on the islet of Käpplingeholmen and burned them alive. Margaret's forces blockaded the town, and from 1392 the dukes of Mecklenburg licensed privateers, the Victual Brothers, to run provisions through; they soon turned to piracy across the whole Baltic. The settlement that freed Albert in 1395 gave him three years either to surrender Stockholm or to pay Margaret a large sum, with the Hanseatic towns holding the town as security in the meantime; he chose to give it up, and it passed to Margaret in 1398, the year after her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania was crowned king of the three kingdoms at Kalmar.

contentSections.title: The union town, 1398–1470
paragraphs: Under the union the castle was a royal fortress held by the king's bailiffs, and the timber town burned often: a fire in the early fifteenth century swept the market place, which was then enlarged, and the town hall on its north side was rebuilt after a fire in 1419. Eric of Pomerania's taxes and his long war with Holstein, which hurt the export of Bergslagen iron, provoked the rising led by the mine-owner Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson from 1434. In April 1436 a rebel force marched on Stockholm, where Eric still had support, and in May Engelbrekt was murdered by a personal enemy.

On 1 May 1436 the council of the realm granted Stockholm a letter of privileges for the loyalty and service its council and commons had shown the realm, the oldest surviving grant of the town's liberties and often taken as the start of its role as capital. Karl Knutsson Bonde, who took over the leadership of the rising, was elected king in June 1448 and ruled as Charles VIII of Sweden. A Danish fleet failed to take the town in 1452. Driven out in 1457, when the rebel leaders had Christian I of Denmark elected in Turku and then in Stockholm, Charles came back in 1464 and again in 1467, died in Stockholm on 15 May 1470 and was buried in the Greyfriars church.

contentSections.title: Sten Sture and Brunkeberg
paragraphs: Charles left his nephew Sten Sture in charge of his lands, including Stockholm and its castle, and a meeting at Arboga elected Sture regent on 1 May 1471. Christian I sailed to Stockholm, anchored off Skeppsholmen and camped on the Brunkeberg ridge north of the town. On 10 October 1471 Sture attacked from the west, his kinsman Nils Bosson Sture from the east and Knut Posse from the town itself. Christian was hit in the face by a handgun shot, a detachment of his army was cut off at the convent of Saint Clare, and many of his men drowned when their makeshift bridge to Käpplingeholmen was broken. Most of the men on both sides were Swedes, and the quarrel was as much about the Bergslagen trade with Lübeck as about Danish rule.

The victory secured Sture's regency for a quarter of a century. Tradition says he had prayed to Saint George before the battle, and he commissioned a monumental oak group of Saint George and the Dragon for Storkyrkan, unveiled in 1489 and widely attributed to Bernt Notke of Lübeck, which was also to be the tomb monument of Sture and his wife. In the same years Storkyrkan was rebuilt: between the 1470s and 1496 its chapels were joined into aisles under new high vaults and the church was lengthened to the east, reaching the size it still has. In 1483 the printer Johann Snell, brought from Lübeck, produced in Stockholm the first book printed in Sweden, the Dialogus creaturarum.

contentSections.title: The medieval town
paragraphs: The walled town filled only the high middle of Stadsholmen. Its first wall, raised in the second half of the thirteenth century, probably ran along the line of today's Prästgatan on the west and Baggensgatan on the east, with the castle closing the north end; its towers were gate towers rather than fighting towers, and the eastern Merchants' Gate stood until the 1680s. The streets Västerlånggatan and Österlånggatan ran just outside it. As landfill and the slow rise of the land pushed the shore outward, houses spread beyond the wall in the fourteenth century and a new wall was built further out, near the water; the foundation piles of its Lion Tower were cut in the winter of 1382–1383.

At the centre, where tracks across the island met, lay the market square, recorded as the great square in 1420, with the town hall on its north side and the town well. Köpmangatan, Merchant Street, recorded in 1323, ran east to the fish market, and Skomakargatan, Shoemaker Street, recorded in 1337, ran south. At the southern tip the weighing house on the iron market weighed and taxed iron and grain from Mälaren before it crossed to the cog harbour on the east shore. Excavations have found wooden paving from about 1250 to 1300 under Västerlånggatan and stone paving from the later fourteenth century. The House of the Holy Spirit, a hospital for the sick, poor and old recorded in 1301, stood on Helgeandsholmen by the northern bridge. The population is estimated at about 5,000 in the early fifteenth century and 5,000 to 7,000 by 1500, small beside continental cities but far larger than any other Swedish town.

contentSections.title: The union's last act
paragraphs: The struggle for Stockholm ran on past 1500. King Hans of Denmark defeated Sture's peasant army at Rotebro in 1497, Sture surrendered the town on 6 October and Hans was crowned; when Sture rose again in 1501, Hans's queen Christina of Saxony held the castle until starvation forced its garrison to give up in May 1502. In 1520 Christina Gyllenstierna, widow of Sten Sture the Younger, defended the town for four months against Christian II of Denmark before accepting a letter of amnesty on 7 September.

Christian was anointed in Storkyrkan on 4 November. On 8 November his soldiers seized guests at the palace, and on 9 November a church court under Archbishop Gustav Trolle condemned them as heretics. Over the next two days two bishops, fourteen nobles, three burgomasters, fourteen town councillors and about twenty citizens were executed on the Great Square, 82 people in all according to the chief executioner. The Stockholm Bloodbath made Gustav Vasa, whose father was among the dead, the leader of a new rising, and when he finally took the town in 1523 he found every second house empty.

contentSections.title: Stockholm beyond its walls
paragraphs: Stockholm turned Sweden's metals into its main link with Europe. Iron and copper from Bergslagen, with hides, dried fish, butter and furs, left its harbour for the Hanseatic towns in exchange for salt, cloth, beer, wine, spices and weapons, and its staple right over the Gulf of Bothnia made it the market for Finland and Norrland too. That trade bound Swedish politics to the Hanseatic towns: the German burghers who backed Albert of Mecklenburg in 1389 and the Bergslagen miners who followed Engelbrekt and Sten Sture were defending the same export route by different means.

The union kings learned that Sweden could not be ruled without the town. The privileges of 1436, the victory of 1471 and its monument, and the killings of 1520 made Stockholm the stage on which Sweden's break with the Kalmar Union was fought out and then remembered, and the town that Birger Jarl fortified became the capital of the kingdom that Gustav Vasa rebuilt.

name: Stockholm
summary: The island town at the outlet of Lake Mälaren that Birger Jarl is credited with founding in the 1250s: Sweden's largest medieval town, the port for Bergslagen iron and copper, and the prize every party of the Kalmar Union era had to hold, from the Käpplinge murders of 1389 to Brunkeberg in 1471.

imageInfo.caption: The walled town of Stockholm on its island, from the lower half of the Vädersolstavlan, a copy painted in 1636 of a lost panel of 1535.
imageInfo.creator: Jacob Heinrich Elbfas, copying a lost original traditionally attributed to Urban målare
imageInfo.source: Storkyrkan, Stockholm, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain)
imageInfo.note: The town section of the painting made after the halo display seen over Stockholm on 20 April 1535. Tree-ring dating in 1998 showed the panel is a seventeenth-century copy, but details such as the unfinished east wing of the castle match the 1530s. Storkyrkan and the castle keep stand at the centre and the southern gate towers at right; the two round towers on the Greyfriars islet at left were new, built by Gustav Vasa around 1530.

sectionImages.caption: The Saint George and the Dragon group in Storkyrkan, unveiled in 1489 to commemorate Sten Sture's victory at Brunkeberg, photographed in 2007.
sectionImages.creator: Palickap
sectionImages.note: The oak group, about 3.5 metres tall, is unsigned but widely attributed to the Lübeck sculptor Bernt Notke. Sten Sture commissioned it as a funerary monument for himself and his wife, and the horse carries his arms; reading the dragon as Denmark is a long tradition rather than a documented intention.

sectionImages.caption: Stockholm besieged and the executions of November 1520, in a drawing by Johan Litheim of about 1690 after a woodcut ordered by Gustav Vasa in 1524.
sectionImages.creator: Johan Litheim, after a lost woodcut of 1524
sectionImages.source: Kungliga biblioteket (National Library of Sweden), via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
sectionImages.note: A copy of a copy of Gustav Vasa's propaganda sheet. The upper band shows the island town with Storkyrkan and the castle between the besiegers' camps; the strip below shows the killings on the Great Square. As a hostile image made years later, it is a better guide to the town's layout than to the details of the executions.

timeline.title: Sigtuna sacked
timeline.description: Eastern raiders burn Sigtuna; a chronicle note written about 1410 links this to the founding of Stockholm.

timeline.title: First record
timeline.description: Birger Jarl issues two letters in July and August that are the first to name Stockholm.

timeline.title: Treaty with Hamburg
timeline.description: A trade treaty follows the earlier one with Lübeck, drawing German merchants to the new town.

timeline.title: Town church recorded
timeline.description: The church of Saint Nicholas, later Storkyrkan, is first mentioned; it is consecrated in 1306.

timeline.title: A royal burial
timeline.description: Magnus III of Sweden is buried in the Greyfriars church on its islet.

timeline.title: Blackfriars convent
timeline.description: The Dominican convent at the southern tip of the island is consecrated.

timeline.title: Käpplinge murders
timeline.description: German partisans of Albert of Mecklenburg burn about seventy men of the Swedish party alive.

timeline.title: Town handed to Margaret
timeline.description: After three years as security with the Hanseatic towns, Stockholm passes to Margaret I of Denmark.

timeline.title: Privileges granted
timeline.description: The council of the realm rewards the town's loyalty with its oldest surviving letter of privileges.

timeline.title: Charles VIII elected
timeline.description: Karl Knutsson Bonde is elected king; he later dies in Stockholm in 1470.

timeline.title: Brunkeberg
timeline.description: Sten Sture defeats Christian I of Denmark on the ridge north of the town.

timeline.title: First Swedish printed book
timeline.description: Johann Snell prints the Dialogus creaturarum in Stockholm.

timeline.title: Saint George and the Dragon
timeline.description: Sten Sture's monument to his victory is unveiled in Storkyrkan.

timeline.title: Castle surrenders
timeline.description: Queen Christina of Saxony's starving garrison gives up the castle to Sten Sture.
